title: [Chapitre] IV. Analysis situs (première mouture) : notes manuscrites (10/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from pp. 62-65). Grothendieck is building an axiomatic, order-theoretic 'analysis situs'. There is a set M of basic pieces (elements X), assumed to satisfy conditions C1-C3. There is an ordered set (𝓕, ≤) of 'figures'. Each figure is a Sup of elements of M lying below it, and figures admit finite Sups and non-empty Infs. M splits into connected components M = ∐_{i∈I} M_i, with I = π_0(M). For a figure F, its i-component is F_i = Sup{X ∈ M_i, X ≤ F}. 𝓕_i denotes the figures contained in M_i. Page 63 showed that F ↦ (F_i) is an injective map 𝓕 → ∏_i 𝓕_i, that the order on 𝓕 is induced by the product order, and that each projection 𝓕 → 𝓕_i commutes with finite Sups and non-empty Infs.

This page asks the converse question: given F_i ∈ 𝓕_i for every i, when is there an F ∈ 𝓕 whose i-components are exactly the F_i?
- An obvious necessary condition (figures being finite Sups / 'finite' objects) is that almost all F_i are empty.
- He therefore introduces axiom C4: if X, Y ∈ M lie in disjoint connected components of M, they are 'compatible', i.e. their Sup exists as a figure (presumably a disjoint union). He notes this is necessary and sufficient for the corollaries.
- Cor. 1: the image of 𝓕 → ∏𝓕_i contains every family with F_i = ∅ for almost all i. Take the finite Sup of the non-empty F_i; C4 together with the finite-Sup axiom makes this legitimate.
- Cor. 2: if I is finite, 𝓕 → ∏𝓕_i is a bijection, in fact an order isomorphism.
- Cor. 3: if all figures are 't.f.' (type fini; 'compl. finis' is added in the margin), then so are the figures of each 𝓕_i, and the image is exactly the finitely supported families.

Page 65 proves Cor. 3 from condition 1 and a lemma: F is t.f. iff each F_i is, and almost all F_i are empty. It then introduces the functorial π_0 notation and a strengthened axiom C4 bis, which asks for surjectivity onto the whole product (arbitrary families, not just finitely supported ones).

In modern terms, this is the standard fact that a 'tame' lattice of closed or constructible sets on a space decomposes as the (restricted) product of the lattices on its connected components. It is a lattice-theoretic analogue of 'a space is the coproduct of its connected components'.
errors: Cor. 1 needs more than pairwise compatibility in C4: it also needs that finitely many pairwise-compatible figures (not just elements of M) have a Sup whose components are the given ones. This is presumably supplied by C1/C2 and the commutation of 𝓕→𝓕_i with finite Sups established on p.63. The page leaves this implicit.

The tension between 'I fini' (p.63 margin) and the treatment of infinite I here suggests the finiteness assumption on π_0(M) was being relaxed mid-draft. Cor. 2 and the 'presque tout i' statements are only non-trivial when I is infinite.

ideas.what: Decomposition of the poset/lattice of figures along connected components of M: 𝓕 ↪ ∏ 𝓕_i, with the axiom C4 that pieces in different components are compatible, giving an isomorphism onto finitely supported families (all families if I is finite)
ideas.modern_name: Product decomposition of a lattice of (constructible/definable) sets over connected components; restricted product
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore (lattice theory / general topology); in tame-topology settings implicit in o-minimality literature (van den Dries)
ideas.where_published: The general tame-topology programme is in Esquisse d'un programme §5; this axiomatic 'analysis situs' chapter appears unpublished

ideas.what: Finiteness condition 'de type fini' for figures and its characterisation componentwise
ideas.modern_name: Finiteness of decompositions (finitely many cells/components meeting a definable set)

deep.surprise_reason: A routine bookkeeping step in an axiomatic framework: decomposing figures along connected components. It is correct and standard. The only mild interest is documentary, as evidence of the 1986 axiomatic 'analysis situs' project.
transcription_corrections: 'C'est vrai et suffisant pour la validité des' is more likely 'C'est néc. et suffisant pour la validité des [corollaires]'.
Line 2 'un F_i ∈ 𝓕_i' is correct; the opening reads 'données, (∀ i ∈ I), un F_i ∈ 𝓕_i'.
'Déjà, il le faut aussi pour ... que ∀i ...' reads roughly as 'Déjà, il le faut, pour [que ce soit le cas], que les F_i soient presque tous ∅ vides' (uncertain).
